messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 57
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 66

Charles is a fifty-seven-year-old tutor at a small community learning center. He works with adults preparing for their high school equivalency exams, sitting across a cluttered desk from each student, helping them wrestle with algebra or essay structure. He keeps the door propped open with a doorstop—he always does, even in winter. The cold air feels better than the alternative.

Twenty-three years ago, Charles was a young high school teacher. He lived alone, too much in his head, and had never been good at reading people. After a department gathering, a senior colleague offered him a ride home. Charles accepted, grateful to avoid the bus. The colleague did not drive him home. He pulled into a quiet park, locked the doors, and, without warning, forced himself onto Charles. Charles did not fight. He went still, the way he imagines a rabbit does when a dog pins it. He said nothing. He did not scream. When it was over, the colleague drove him home as if nothing had happened. Charles never told anyone—not the principal, not the police, not even his own mother. He stopped teaching two years later. He could not stomach the hallways, the staff meetings, the way the colleague remained on faculty, greeting him with a confident smile.

Now, Charles tutors. The work feels safer—shorter sessions, no formal authority, no faculty rooms. But safety is a fragile word. When a student leans too far across the desk, reaching for a pencil or to point at a page, Charles flinches. He tries to cover it by shifting in his chair or pretending to cough. He has learned to stand during tutoring, keeping the desk between himself and the student. He never touches anyone. A student once reached out to thank him, her hand brushing his shoulder, and he pulled back so quickly that she stared. He said he was sorry—he was a “jumpy guy.” He feels the shame hours later, replaying the moment in his head.

At night, Charles does not sleep well. He lies in bed with the light on, his back to the wall, facing the door. He wakes from dreams he cannot fully recall—just a heaviness, the sense of a hand on his mouth. He walks to the kitchen, pours a glass of whiskey, and sips it until his pulse slows. He never finishes the bottle, but he comes close. The next day, he tutors with a dull headache, snapping at students who ask for help a second time. He apologizes quickly, explaining that he did not sleep well. He has used that excuse for so many years that it no longer sounds like an excuse, just a fact.

He has stopped going to the grocery store late at night. Sometimes a man walking too close behind him in line triggers a racing heart, a wave of heat, the urge to bolt. He scans parking lots before exiting his car. He scans every room he enters. He does not call it scanning—he calls it “being aware.” He does not date. He tried once, five years ago, but the first kiss sent him into a full-blown panic, tears streaming, the woman confused and then angry. He stopped trying.

This morning, a student asked him to close the door so they could concentrate. Charles felt his chest tighten. He said no—the door stays open, that is the policy. The truth is, there is no policy. The student shrugged, but Charles could not shake the feeling of being trapped. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood in a stall, breathing through his mouth, waiting for the nausea to pass. He stared at the tiled floor and thought, *I am fifty-seven years old. I am still afraid of a door.*
